technique_library.when_to_use: Any fact, date or headline figure that can belong to an object or place; naming groups, places and topics without captions.
how_to_execute: Choose the object or surface that would naturally carry the word.
Letter it in the scene's style on that surface plane, in the accent colour for key numbers.
Write, pop, count up or reveal it (by a turn, a pan or a character passing) as it is spoken.
Keep it to one to three words or a number, and hold long enough to read.
Optionally hand the readout to the next idea (morph into a map or route).
technique_library.timing: draw_on median 1.0 s; signage text median 0.05 of frame height (p10 0.03, p90 0.1); number height median 0.08 (p75 0.12); reveals by turn or pan about 1 to 2 s; holds 2 to 12 s.
technique_library.loom_notes: Object states and Loom.ui artefacts carry real words, counters exist, and the iso kit places text on planes. Missing: hand-lettered numeral fonts with stroke order, sign and window surfaces as place props, and a rig back-view for text revealed by a turn.

technique_library.name: A small accent traveller follows a drawn route
technique_library.description: A small subject, often the only accent-coloured thing in a muted, static field, travels a drawn route: a vehicle on a dashed map line, a microbe down a tube, a book across lands, a figure between two groups or through a crowd.
technique_library.when_to_use: Journeys, routes, changes of side, anomalies, the spread of an idea, a single case moving through a system.
how_to_execute: Build the static field in the base palette and draw the route first (dashed line, tube, road).
Give only the traveller the accent colour.
Move it along the route with an ease-in-out.
Pop a pin or label on arrival.
Let the camera drift with it only when the route leaves the frame; optionally end on a still close-up of the traveller.
technique_library.timing: Path-follow medians 1.63 to 2.29 s (p25 1.13 s, p75 3.4 to 4.0 s, p90 6.59 s); walk-cycle medians 2.96 to 3.42 s.
technique_library.loom_notes: Travel along paths exists; walk cycles are basic.

technique_library.name: Near-black mode for the inner, microscopic or unknown
technique_library.description: Abstract, microscopic, inner-mind or unknown beats switch the film into a near-black or navy void with one light line colour or one glowing subject and sparse drifting specks, then return to the lit world. A variant fills a character's head silhouette with the void and pins colour-blocked regions or a glowing core inside it.
technique_library.when_to_use: Unknowns and open questions, inside-the-body or inside-the-system beats, mental states and cognition, a solemn verdict.
how_to_execute: Switch the field to near-black or navy (by cut, dissolve, or a morph of a head into a silhouette).
Draw with one light line colour, or one subject with a soft outer glow instead of an outline.
Add sparse drifting specks for life; use neon line-on-black for any data in this mode.
Pin labels on regions as they are named.
Return to the warm illustrated world by a dissolve or hard cut.
technique_library.timing: Void beats run from 0.6 s transitions to 14.6 s explanations (inner-world shots of 2 to 15 s); void_dark backgrounds in 54 shots across 10 films of one batch and in 9 of 12 films of another.
technique_library.loom_notes: Dark packs (cinematic-noir, dark-technical, glow-flat) render the look, and silhouettes, particles and labels exist. Missing: a mid-lesson mode switch to a void register inside a light pack such as editorial-paper.

technique_library.name: Population grid: accent the subset, then single out one
technique_library.description: A population is a uniform grid or row of identical figures or units; a share is marked by the accent (tint, cross, starburst, a wiped panel, sliced sectors), often with the number stamped across an empty band or no number at all, and the grid then collapses or zooms to one specimen to move from the many to the case.
technique_library.when_to_use: Prevalence, survey results, share of a team, adoption across a population, and moving from 'many cases' to 'this one case'.
how_to_execute: Tile one simple figure or unit edge to edge on a flat field; hold briefly for 'many'.
Mark the affected share with the accent on the word, or change its faces or state marks with a stagger.
Optionally leave a horizontal empty band and stamp the number or word in it.
Recolour or scale up one unit and fade the rest, or push into one figure, or collapse the grid into a lens on one specimen.
Act on the one (label it, highlight it) and hold it as the new subject.
technique_library.timing: Grid holds about 4.6 s before the collapse; grid beats 7 to 9 s; wipe in median 0.8 s, fade in median 0.54 s, scale in median 0.58 s (code); push-ins of about 6.4 s follow.
technique_library.loom_notes: Unit grids, seeded arrays, recolour, scale and camera push exist. A stamped-band layout and sliced face circles would be small template parameters. Shares must come from the source.

technique_library.name: Motif wave wipe that settles into a flat brand-colour end field
technique_library.description: The last transition is the film's motif shape (a smooth or organic wave in the brand colour) sweeping the frame; it settles into a flat two or three colour field (brand colour, white, black) with one tiny subject and one slow action, the credits bar slides in, and the colour may later drain back to a clean field.
technique_library.when_to_use: Closing a lesson with an authored, brand-consistent gesture rather than a cut to black, especially when the transition itself can be the final metaphor or when a textured film needs a decisive tonal break.
how_to_execute: Establish the band or wave shape once earlier as a motif.
Sweep it across the frame in one eased move (fast start, slow settle), swallowing the last scene.
Reduce the palette to the brand colour, white and black; draw one large flat shape (sea, landmass, grid) and one tiny dark subject.
Give the subject one small action or a slow path, and fade drifting ambient elements in step with the wipe so the field ends clean.
Slide in the fixed credits bar and hold.
Optionally drain the colour back to a clean field with a smooth ease-out under the bar.
technique_library.timing: Wave or wipe shots 2.0 to 3.2 s (wipe-in median about 0.8 s, p90 2.4 s); the settled field holds about 8.5 to 20 s of credits; drain about 3 s.
technique_library.loom_notes: Wipe join, flat fields and ambient motion exist; an organic or wave wipe edge taken from the pack or brand file, an accent-colour fill and a colour-drain parameter are missing. Use the client's brand colour and shape, never this channel's red device.

technique_library.name: One element carries across the cut
technique_library.description: A moving or held element continues across a join with matched screen position and direction (a ball's arc, a card in a hand, a cursor, a butterfly, a torch, a pose reused for a reframe, hands that slide off and become the entrance), so a change of setting reads as travel and the eye never loses the subject.
technique_library.when_to_use: Moving between places or registers that share an idea while keeping one subject in view, such as a document travelling between departments, or whenever two shots should read as one gesture or one person.
how_to_execute: Choose the carrier (an object, a hand, a pose, a light, a small living element) and set it moving before the join.
Match its screen position, scale and direction on both sides of the join, or let it exit toward one edge and enter from the matching edge.
Cut on its motion, timed to the spoken keyword, or hold it in place through a dissolve while the world changes beneath it.
Let its move continue briefly into the new shot, then land it on the next keyword.
technique_library.timing: The carrier's move continues about 0.3 to 1 s into the new shot; path-follow median about 1.6 to 3 s, with single carries up to about 14.5 s.
technique_library.loom_notes: Travel along paths and the travel join exist inside or between stations; persisting one element's position and motion across two stations while everything else changes needs a shared-element parameter at the join.

technique_library.name: Repeating pattern fills and motif bands set the place
technique_library.description: Walls, water, ground, floors and backgrounds are filled with small repeating patterns or one decorative motif band (a meander border for antiquity, horizontal bands for water, a checkerboard floor as a neutral stage, a tiled wall) that imply material and era without shading, perspective or detailed backgrounds.
technique_library.when_to_use: Dense storybook worlds; setting era or place in one stroke; filling negative space with texture.
how_to_execute: Choose one motif or two to three pattern tiles that signal the place.
Run them as flat bands, floors or large surface fills at low contrast so they read as texture.
Repeat the same motif across all scenes of that place.
Keep figures plain so they read against the pattern.
technique_library.timing: Static and persistent; pattern backgrounds in 83 shots across 11 films of one batch.
technique_library.loom_notes: Pattern fills and motif bands are not in the pack list; needs pattern tiles (meander, bands, checkerboard, tiles) as pack elements.

technique_library.name: Short reset beat: dark void, flat field or calm image
technique_library.description: A sub-second to roughly three-second beat with no new information resets attention: a near-black field with one glowing line, burst or word on a single spoken word, a flat colour slowly deepening, a dip to black then a bright streak, a full-frame brightness ramp, or a calm static human moment.
technique_library.when_to_use: Between dense technical ideas, at a 'but', a phase change, a topic pivot, a long time jump, an open question, the end of a list, or the single biggest dramatic beat.
how_to_execute: Hard cut, or soft join (white fade, push), to the reset image.
Use a near-black or flat field with at most one shape, or a calm image with one accent and no labels.
Let only a slow tone shift, one line of light or one word move, landing on its spoken word if any.
Do not narrate new facts over it.
Leave within about a second for punctuation, a little longer for a breather.
Use a dip to black at most once per film; cluster two or three dark beats only to mark a series of open questions.
technique_library.timing: Dark punctuation 0.6 to 1.2 s (FKUc8vg_Lus s016 0.6 s, NOaeKRft-gc s049 1.2 s); rest beats 0.6 to 1.4 s; brightness ramp shot 0.6 s; breathers 0.6 to 2.8 s.
technique_library.loom_notes: Authorable as a short station with dip, fade, stamp or light-grow; the 'shock' join meaning fits. Conflict to resolve: Loom's empty-frame check flags these deliberate rest beats, so it needs an explicit allow marker on the beat. The narration must leave room for it.

technique_library.name: Outlined foreground over ghosted, low-contrast background
technique_library.description: Characters and hero props carry a uniform dark outline and full-weight line; backgrounds and secondary figures are outline-free, paler, thinner or single-hue line art in a narrow value range, so the active figure always reads first while the setting stays constant.
technique_library.when_to_use: Any illustrated scene with a place behind the actor, especially a constant setting that holds a spoken list of people.
how_to_execute: Outline figures and hero props at one weight with flat fills.
Draw background shapes with no outline (or thin pale single-hue line) at reduced opacity and a narrow value range.
Swap foreground figures on each spoken item while the ghosted setting stays constant.
Fade rear crowd figures into a dense pale mass to sell depth.
Use a dark foreground element only to frame, never to compete.
technique_library.timing: Static rule; foreground swaps on each spoken item.
technique_library.loom_notes: Depth layers exist but packs set one outline style for all layers; needs a per-layer outline policy (figure, prop, background) with line weight and opacity so packs can ghost the back layer.

technique_library.name: First scene ghosts in under the card or lifts from a white wash
technique_library.description: The hand-off from the opening text card to the world is gradual: the first illustration fades up faintly behind the outgoing quote, or lifts from a white or pale wash into a hazy, low-contrast establishing view, before the first story shot.
technique_library.when_to_use: Any hand-off from a text card to a scene, above all the opening card to the first image, so text eases into picture without a hard cut.
how_to_execute: Keep the outgoing card's field colour.
Start the incoming scene at very low opacity behind the text in the last part of the card, or under a near-white overlay.
Fade the text out while the scene rises to full contrast, or lift the white overlay over about 0.5 s.
Keep the establishing view low contrast and desaturated at first.
Cut to the first character or story shot once the scene has resolved.
technique_library.timing: Fade-in median about 0.54 s; one establishing shot runs 0.6 s (6.0 to 6.6 s) before the first story cut; a white wash resolves over about 1 s in another film.
technique_library.loom_notes: Fade and dip joins exist. The deliberate overlap of quote text and a faint scene would be flagged by Loom's double-exposure check, and a white first frame would trip the poster or empty-frame check; both are conflicts to resolve with an allowed-overlap flag for card hand-offs, not defects of the films.

technique_library.name: Cross-dissolve chain of vignettes through one shared ground
technique_library.description: Small self-contained vignettes on the same paper or field colour dissolve one into the next through bare ground, so very different scenes, a list or an escalation read as one surface being redrawn.
technique_library.when_to_use: Enumerating examples, steps of an escalation, a compressed historical arc, or linking a person to a place inside one hand-made world.
how_to_execute: Build each vignette as a small centred drawing on the same ground colour and texture.
Keep one warm accent on the focal item of each vignette.
Fade the outgoing drawing to bare ground and fade the next one up from it, starting on the clause boundary.
Hold each vignette long enough to read.
technique_library.timing: Dissolves about 0.5 to 1 s (fade-in median 0.5 to 0.58 s, exit fade median 0.7 s); vignettes held several seconds between dissolves.
technique_library.loom_notes: Fade and dissolve joins exist; build the vignettes as layers of one station so the ground never changes. Loom's double-exposure check may flag the mid-dissolve frames; the overlap is on bare ground and brief, so the check should treat it as a dissolve, not a defect.

technique_library.name: Slow tilt up to a light or down to a hidden level
technique_library.description: One continuous slow tilt carries the eye vertically: down from sky or canopy to ground or underground to discover a hidden level, or up from a grounded subject (onlookers, a pile of the fallen) through parallax layers to a skyline or one bright source for a hopeful or epic turn.
technique_library.when_to_use: Tilt down: discovery of a hidden level, context to detail. Tilt up: hopeful or epic turns, revealing scale above a scene.
how_to_execute: Build a tall canvas with the start subject at one end and the destination at the other.
Tilt slowly in one continuous eased move through the parallax layers.
Land on the subject or the bright focal source as it is named.
technique_library.timing: Tilt shots about 2.2 to 12.7 s; tilt down tagged in 15 shots across 9 films of one batch.
technique_library.loom_notes: Camera move on a tall canvas, or between vertically stacked stations, exists.

technique_library.name: One colour bound to one meaning for the whole film
technique_library.description: Beyond the focal accent, each recurring concept, entity or side of a polarity keeps one fixed hue for the whole film (red for the threat, gold only on authority, oxygen blue and hydrogen pink, warm versus cool poles, one costume accent per recurring speaker), so the colour becomes a label and diagrams read without a legend.
technique_library.when_to_use: Films that track one agent, risk or idea through many scenes and scales; topics with a small set of recurring entities (gases, roles, teams, systems); any two-way comparison or polarity held across a film.
how_to_execute: List the recurring concepts or entities and assign one hue each before any scene is drawn.
For a two-way comparison, pick one warm and one cool hue and place the pair symmetrically left and right.
Use each hue only on its concept, on every icon, particle, label, stream and character detail alike.
Never use those hues for decoration, the background or crowds, and never swap the mapping later.
Add labels only after the colours have done the separating.
technique_library.timing: Film-wide; no duration.
technique_library.loom_notes: Pack palette and brand tokens exist; missing is a lesson-level semantic colour map (concept to pack token) that scene builders must read and a lint that flags a mapped hue on an unmapped element.

technique_library.name: People, crowds and threats as flat silhouettes
technique_library.description: Crowds, operators, authorities and threats are flat featureless silhouettes (near-black or one flat colour), sometimes with a thin glowing rim on dark fields, looping two or three gestures; the one figure that matters is drawn in full colour or given the only accent, white fill or rim. Pose, not face, carries emotion.
technique_library.when_to_use: Collectives, public reaction, users, teams, unknown authorities, menace, serious segments and any crowd that would cost detail; isolating one actor from many.
how_to_execute: Fill the figures solid near-black or one flat field colour with no interior detail.
Place them on a soft radial or vertical gradient, or add a thin pale rim stroke, for edge contrast.
Stagger a two or three pose loop across a crowd; keep it near static.
Draw only the subject in full colour, or give it the only accent, white fill or rim colour.
Show operators from behind so the screen they face is the subject.
Resolve a silhouette into a coloured named figure on the spoken name if it becomes a person.
Cut from the wide mass to a tight isolated figure to dramatise many to one.
technique_library.timing: Silhouette impact beats 0.8 to 2.4 s; silhouette processions and group drifts hold 5 to 10 s (walk cycles median 1.75 s, code).
technique_library.loom_notes: Fills are pack-driven and seeded arrays and staggered groups exist, so a crowd can be built. Missing: a silhouette shading mode on rigs (solid fill plus optional rim stroke and accent eyes) and an isolate-one parameter. Glowing eyes and monster silhouettes read as menace; for employees prefer plain silhouettes with one accent.

technique_library.name: The subject object gets a minimal face
technique_library.description: An inanimate thing or component (a folder, a cell, an organ, a material, a device, a metronome) keeps its real silhouette and gains two dot eyes and one curve, sometimes thin stick arms, so it can carry strain or relief; its expression changes with its state and it may act out each property with one prop.
technique_library.when_to_use: Making a tool, a file, a component or a material approachable; showing strain or relief inside a system; explaining properties of a thing with no natural actor.
how_to_execute: Keep the object's real silhouette and add two dot eyes and one curve, nothing more.
Map states to three expressions: neutral, strained, relieved.
Change the expression on the word that names the effect.
Optionally give it thin arms (never legs) and hand it one prop per property.
Keep the face small so the diagram still reads as a diagram.
Keep the same design for the whole film.
technique_library.timing: character_act median 0.5 to 0.63 s (code); a whole property demonstration runs within a 10.6 s shot; single emotional beats 2.4 to 3.4 s.
technique_library.loom_notes: Object families have states but no face layer; a small face kit (eyes, brows, mouth curves) attachable to any object grammar would cover most uses. Arms and props make it an object-mascot rig, which is a new primitive. Use with restraint for corporate learners: a face on a document or a tool reads friendly; a cute mascot on a serious compliance point can read childish.

technique_library.name: Diagram assembled part by part as the parts are named
technique_library.description: A mechanism or system diagram is built on one held frame in the order the narration names its parts, starting from the bare central object, so the viewer builds the machine in step with the voice; connecting lines are drawn only after both of their ends exist.
technique_library.when_to_use: Mechanisms, procedures and system diagrams.
how_to_execute: Write the narration so parts are named in assembly order.
Start from the bare central object on a held frame.
Bring each part in on its word with a pop, slide or draw-on.
Draw connecting lines only after both ends exist.
Hold the finished assembly before the next idea.
technique_library.timing: Builds run about 10 to 16 s on one held frame (QyRqlTV60zM s073 14.8 s, ul-c6a4QkiU s020b 15.9 s); pop-in median 0.5 s, draw-on median 0.67 s per part.
technique_library.loom_notes: Word timings drive cues. Missing: a gate that fails any part appearing before its word and any connector drawn before both ends exist (seen in QyRqlTV60zM s070 and P5pmMe3EarI s041).

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: comparison (two conditions, two outcomes, variation or universality)
explanation_patterns.device: equal split panels or mirrored subjects that vary one element
explanation_patterns.recipe: Divide the frame with a thin gutter or hard edge, or stand both items on one shared baseline, and place the same subject at the same scale and pose on each side; colour-code the sides warm and cool. Establish the pictures first, then change only the variable under test and pop each side's number or effect icon on its spoken value, with labels last. Resolve with one gesture: slide the loser away, strike the rejected cause, or tip a balance beam. For 'it varies', demote the hero to one tile among variants; for 'it is universal', play one gesture in sync across differently coloured cells. A single object morphing in place under a fixed term band is the one-frame variant.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: quantity (a large count, volume or 'many')
explanation_patterns.device: repeated identical units that accumulate
explanation_patterns.recipe: Design one small unit that reads at tiny size and show it alone first. Stagger identical copies in, timed to the spoken count, into a row, grid, ring, stack or onto a map or silhouette until the set reads as many; switch to smaller markers when it gets dense. Hold the full set still, or pull back to show its extent, or drift the camera along a row so more is implied than shown. Reorganise or remove units to show change, or cross-dissolve the same units into a familiar place so the number becomes concrete. Use units instead of an on-screen figure unless the figure must be stated.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: structure (what is inside, its parts and layers)
explanation_patterns.device: cutaway, unfold or magnifier with each part named on its word
explanation_patterns.recipe: Show the closed whole first. Open it on the naming word: split it into a cross-section, unfold it, turn it translucent, explode it along one axis, or tie a circular lens to the exact spot with a leader line. Reduce the body or object to a flat silhouette container, fill the named region with the accent and pop a short label with at most one leader line exactly on the spoken name; for stacks, add one layer per named part over a constant reference line and keep a small figure for scale. Cross-fade lens content per sub-idea, close the lens or swap back to the whole when the sentence ends.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: scale (one part of a much larger or much smaller system)
explanation_patterns.device: one continuous camera move between levels
explanation_patterns.recipe: To go up a level, start on one hero object or a private detail and pull back in one continuous move until it is one of many identical copies, a tile in a lattice, a speck in a vast field or a ring of figures on a globe; flatten the receding copies to silhouettes and keep a small human for scale. To go down a level, push through an opening in the familiar surface (a cell, a screen, a skin) into a darker micro field, carry the accent colour through, let specks resolve into agents, type the term on as the scale lands, then pull back to the whole system.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: spread, route or journey across a territory or system
explanation_patterns.device: a muted map as a stage with one accent path and one marker per place
explanation_patterns.recipe: Flatten the map or system to two muted tones with thin labels and hold it still. Pop one uniform marker per spoken place in the warm accent, staggered in the direction of spread, and stamp the year when it matters; or grow one accent ribbon, dashed line or moving dot along the route in travel order, landing the arrowhead on the destination as it is named. Mark stopped advances with X stamps, grow a region in small steps per clause, and keep a small corner locator when the path goes deep inside a system.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: quantity (one headline statistic or an extreme magnitude)
explanation_patterns.device: the number set on a physical object, a counter that locks, or a swap to a familiar object
explanation_patterns.recipe: Clear to one field and set the number large on or beside an object from the story (a sign, a bag, a container, a stopwatch). Roll a counter and lock it on the spoken value, filling a container or scaling the object in steps as it climbs; pop any emphasis burst only after the lock. Nest a subset inside the numeral or add one small figure enacting the measured behaviour. For extreme magnitudes, cross-dissolve the subject into a familiar object on the comparison word and hand-write the multiplier beside it, then dissolve back. Every figure comes from the source.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: history (a sequence of eras, owners or versions)
explanation_patterns.device: a constant anchor while the era swaps around it
explanation_patterns.recipe: Hold the character or key object in the same pose and position and cross-fade only the background props and room, or swap one attribute (a flag's colours, hair) per spoken era, or swap the old version into exactly the same position with callouts unmoved. Alternatively lay the eras as vignettes or framed panels along one wide strip and reveal them with one continuous pan, popping the year in a reserved colour on its mention and introducing people with a typed nameplate. Shift the palette to an era colour and keep a fixed year tag.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: feeling or inner state (as a sign on or over the person)
explanation_patterns.device: externalised symbol, glowing marks or a glowing double
explanation_patterns.recipe: Keep the figure still, reduced and in a matching posture, or a featureless dark silhouette on a saturated field. Grow one accent symbol out of or over it in stages timed to the words (a flame from the head, a watching eye, a lit chest, a scribble knot, a burst at the pain site), or pop small bright marks inside it; for a real speaker, wrap a wobbly glowing outline round them. An inner voice or ideal can be a soft glowing silhouette beside the crisp person that changes shape for each turn. Let the pose do the rest and clear the symbol when the state resolves.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: process (an invisible actor doing several steps)
explanation_patterns.device: personification: one small character, or one worker per step
explanation_patterns.recipe: Make the invisible actor one small character with a fixed silhouette, colour, face grammar and one prop, name it once with a written label, and let it physically perform every step (carry, read, tick, squeeze, operate) while bystanders react, so the cause is read from their faces; it stays the same character for the whole film. When there are several actors, split the narration into clauses and cast one small figure per clause with one job prop, animating only that job on a central object that transforms in place. An administrative procedure can be the same: one figure, one recurring prop, one physical action per spoken step.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: feeling or power (as space and scale around the person)
explanation_patterns.device: a small figure in a vast or dominating field
explanation_patterns.recipe: Put one small faceless figure low in a large dark, empty or flat field with a single soft glow or slow falling particles, and hold the camera still so only the atmosphere moves; let weather or closing frames track the intensity. For pressure or power, let a large figure, force or hand fill the rest of the frame with rim light on its silhouette, or a soft shadow loom beside the person.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: misconception or claim (being judged, revised or corrected)
explanation_patterns.device: state the claim, hold it, then negate or correct it in place
explanation_patterns.recipe: Write or stage the claim or myth literally and hold it long enough to be believed. On the word that introduces the problem, draw a red strike-through, a scribble or a bold X over it, or slam a tilted stamp or prohibition symbol in the accent only, keeping the original visible; swap the corrected word into the same line, or cut to the evidence. When the claim is a model, keep its labels attached and morph its structure into the correct one in a single move, then hold the result as fact.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: duration, frequency or a deadline
explanation_patterns.device: a still subject under a changing cycle
explanation_patterns.recipe: Lock the subject and change only one cycling element: the sky's palette with a moving sun or moon, a water level rising and falling, ticks crossing off a calendar, a window turning day to night, or a clock whose hands turn with the narration. Let the viewer count repetitions instead of reading a number, keep one tiny secondary motion alive, and mark a deadline by freezing every figure on the strike. For a span, draw an arrow on under the subject in sync with the spoken length and land the number at its tip.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: quantity (a share, prevalence or one case among many)
explanation_patterns.device: uniform grid of identical figures with an accented subset, then one singled out
explanation_patterns.recipe: Lay out identical figures or units evenly on a flat field. On the word, tint, cross, wipe or slice the affected share in the accent, or change its faces or state marks with a stagger; stamp the percentage or a word across an empty band, or show no number at all. To move from group to case, push the camera into one unit until it fills the frame, or flag it with the accent and a short halo, and hold it as the new subject.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: process (a change of state over time in one subject)
explanation_patterns.device: draw it once, then change it in place
explanation_patterns.recipe: Draw the scene or the subject once, centred in a fixed set, and never redraw it. Show each stage as an in-place change tied to its spoken word: a colour wash creeping over the affected area, a fill or colour swap on a fixed cutaway, one dark shape growing over a long hold, accent particles bunching where a channel narrows, or the subject morphing through named states (ingredient to product, healthy to failed). For a collapse, hold the intact object about two seconds, then snap it to the new state so it completes on the spoken result. Instant swaps (X-eyes, a badge's text) suit sensitive outcomes. Hold the end state.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: list (named items, roles, causes or qualities)
explanation_patterns.device: one item per spoken word, in one place
explanation_patterns.recipe: Lay out empty slots or the diagram the items belong to, then fill them one per spoken name: icons of one family pop in a row with a one-word label, regions on a diagram light with a colour-matched bullet, or the glyph inside one fixed central container swaps per keyword. Keep the accent on the current item, truck slowly along long rows, end with a highlight on the key item, and clear the set before showing the exception.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: invisible force, signal or measurement
explanation_patterns.device: the force as the only saturated element: rings, a glowing line or a light beam
explanation_patterns.recipe: Switch to a plain or near-black field and draw the machine or scene flat or as wireframe. Reserve one accent hue for the signal and make it the only saturated thing: thin rings that pulse from the source, a glowing line that traces the flow, or a wedge or beam of light that sweeps a dark mass. Reveal, recolour or warm each object only when the signal reaches it, so the change has a visible cause; let findings accumulate as dots before any warning stamps. Collapse or flatten the rings to reset.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: relationships and networks (roles, stakeholders, loops)
explanation_patterns.device: node-and-line network built hub first
explanation_patterns.recipe: Fill one small outlined shape to become the hub, then pop the surrounding nodes in a stagger on the spoken list, or reveal evenly spaced satellites with a pull-out from the hub. Draw the connecting lines only after every node is present; add faces or link symbols after the structure is built, and mark the decision-maker with the accent. For a reciprocal loop between two parties, draw the first arrow when the first action happens and the return arrow only after the response.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: structure or making process (parts combined in order)
explanation_patterns.device: build the whole left to right in the order it is named
explanation_patterns.recipe: On a paper sheet or flat field, draw or bring in each part or step only when it is named, left to right, each snapping in with a small settle; give each part type its own shape and reuse that shape family in every later diagram. Reserve the accent for the risky or decisive step, and bring the user or the finished product in last.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: rule, policy or principle (an abstraction with no picture)
explanation_patterns.device: a physical apparatus or one object doing one action
explanation_patterns.recipe: Make the rule a machine or object the viewer can watch work: a booth that slices value off, a drum that drops one ball, a scroll that unrolls, a figure that steps out of bounds on a bare stage with one ground line. Isolate it in a soft light pool or on a flat field, run exactly one action from start to finish on the narration and mark the result with the accent. For an analogy, align the metaphor and the real thing on one axis, show the principle on the metaphor, then dissolve through a shared outline into the real thing while the principle overlay stays.

explanation_patterns.concept_kind: definition (naming a term)
explanation_patterns.device: the term isolated on a bare field, then the concrete thing appears
explanation_patterns.recipe: Isolate the term in large display type on one plain or saturated field, lettering it on as it is spoken; then let the concrete thing surface under it, or present the subject as a labelled exhibit on a plinth whose nameplate completes as the term is said. To generalise, morph one concrete example into a ring of small varied examples around the category word. Open into the scene once the term has landed.

rules.rule: Keep one saturated accent hue in the frame and put it on the element the narration is naming; everything else stays muted, desaturated or in one cool family. The exceptions are the brand card and credits, a fixed colour code (one hue per entity), the two sides of a comparison, and deliberate abundance or chaos beats.
rules.measurable_as: Per frame outside the brand card and credits: cluster pixels above a high-chroma threshold by hue; pass at one accent cluster (more only when each extra hue is a declared code or comparison side) whose box overlaps the element named in the current beat's word timings. Colour accent is the top focal cue in every batch, on about a third to a half of shots (0.33 to 0.49 per batch). Accents are named by the vision model, not measured, so calibrate the chroma threshold on frames.

rules.rule: The accent moves with the narration: when a new element is named it takes the accent, and the previous one returns to the field family.
rules.measurable_as: Timeline against Loom word timings: the accent-coloured element id changes within about 1 s of the word naming the new element (batch 04 colour changes run a median 1.13 s); on each word-synced pop-in the new element holds the frame's maximum saturation.

rules.rule: A colour bound to a meaning or an entity keeps it for the whole film (one hue for the threat, one per recurring entity, one for time markers) and is never swapped or reused as decoration.
rules.measurable_as: Storyboard declares a concept-to-hue map; lint any beat where a mapped hue sits on an element not tagged with that concept, or where one concept uses two hues.

rules.rule: Plan the palette as a colour script: the dominant field colour changes at section boundaries (one field family per section, neighbours differ) while the accent role, the ground texture and recurring figures' colours stay constant. Mark a new segment by changing the field, not by adding scenery, and end on the brand neutral.
rules.measurable_as: Dominant background hue cluster per section: stable inside a section, different from its neighbour; the records list about 7 to 10 colour-script segments per film (batches 05 and 06); recurring character fills identical across segments; element count at a boundary stays near the shot median; final field near white or the brand neutral.

rules.rule: Shade flat: cel fills or none, and no gradient shading on characters; soft gradients only in sky bands, lamp glows or a soft highlight, with any other volume from halftone or a flat offset shadow.
rules.measurable_as: Shading tags flat_cel or none on 657 of 799 shots (batch 02) and 921 of 1068 (batch 06); measure fill variance inside character masks and the share of smooth-gradient pixels outside the top band of the frame.

rules.rule: Labels that must be read sit at about 0.05 of frame height and do not go below about 0.03.
rules.measurable_as: OCR text height / frame height: label median 0.05 in batches 01 to 07 and 0.07 in batch 08; the batch p10 floors range from 0.025 to 0.04. Flag any meaning-bearing label below 0.03.

rules.rule: Titles, section cards and term cards are large and alone, one or two lines, in heavy negative space; an opening quote sits smaller under the brand title.
rules.measurable_as: Title text height median 0.12 to 0.18 of frame across batches (p25 0.06 to 0.12; never below 0.08 in batch 08); term cards at least 0.1 high and at most 2 lines; opening quote 0.06 to 0.08.

rules.rule: A number that carries the beat is set larger than the labels around it (about two to three times label height) and sits on an object in the world, such as a sign, tag, counter or bar.
rules.measurable_as: Number text median 0.08 to 0.12 of frame height in batches 01, 02, 03, 06 and 07 against labels at 0.05; hero numbers 0.18 to 0.35 (batch 08). Batch 04 measured numbers at label size (median 0.05), so the ratio is usual, not universal.

rules.rule: Text below about 0.03 of frame height is secondary texture only (credits, UI, signage, or diagram detail next to a larger label), never information the viewer must read.
rules.measurable_as: Text under 0.03 of frame height is of kind credits, ui_text, signage or diagram_text; credits median 0.03 (p10 0.02); batch 07 diagram text reaches p10 0.015, the one place these films go smaller; fail meaning-bearing text below 0.02.

rules.rule: On-screen text is a word, a term, a number or a short label, never a narration sentence or a bullet list; sentences appear only on the opening quote card, in the credits, or on an artefact in the world.
rules.measurable_as: Words per text block at most 3 to 4 outside title, quote and credits cards (batches 03 and 04); list-type text in only a few shots per batch (4 of 640 in batch 01, 4 of 1068 in batch 06); text echo of the narration in 41 of 640 shots (batch 01); share of shots with any text 0.10 to 0.53 per film, story films under 0.20 (batch 08).

rules.rule: Put text on something: an object surface, sign, tag, screen, backing card or band, or hand-letter it in the art's line; not loose caption strips over the scene. Text that must be read in full lives on a document or board written on with the voice.
rules.measurable_as: Every text box has an opaque backing or lies inside an object's bounding box; text kinds signage, label and diagram_text outnumber caption 260 to 26 (batch 05).

rules.rule: Text and overlays sit in negative space beside the subject and never cover a face or the focal object.
rules.measurable_as: Bounding boxes of text or overlays do not intersect detected face boxes or the focal object's box.

rules.rule: A label sits on the thing it names, arrives on its word and clears before the next label or idea; labels never pile up into a legend, and keys and leader lines are avoided.
rules.measurable_as: Label box touches or overlaps its target; onset inside the target word's interval (Loom word timings); no overlay from beat n still visible after the first new overlay of beat n+1 enters.

rules.rule: Faces stay minimal (dot eyes, an arc, one exaggerated feature, or blank), and emotion is carried by posture, one gesture, the head and brows, and the accent.
rules.measurable_as: Rig property: face features limited to eyes, one mouth line and brows, with no face shading beyond one split; judgement for the pose read.

rules.rule: Animated characters do not talk on camera: no lip sync; the off-screen narrator carries the words.
rules.measurable_as: No mouth-shape track on drawn rigs; lip sync in 2 to 13 shots per batch, nearly all live action (all 4 in batch 03).

rules.rule: Keep characters few: one actor carries each beat.
rules.measurable_as: Characters per shot median 1 in every batch; p90 3 to 4 in most batches (6 in batch 05, 8 in batch 01 where crowds appear); flag beats above 4 unless the extra figures are a repeated crowd.

rules.rule: Acting is short snaps: one pose or gesture change per beat, landing on the stressed word, then held; not continuous performance.
rules.measurable_as: character_act median 0.5 to 1.0 s across batches (p75 1.5 to 2.4 s); one main gesture per character beat with its peak inside the stressed word's interval (Loom word timings).

rules.rule: A recurring character or abstract agent keeps one design, one silhouette and one accent for the whole film; a change of state is a pose, expression or colour swap on the same figure, not a new character.
rules.measurable_as: Character id maps to one rig id and one accent across all beats; the same design recurs in at least 3 to 4 shots of its sections.

rules.rule: Show death, injury, violence and destruction by symbol: one snappy motion plus a flat colour mark, a small burst, X eyes, a flash or a fade of light, then a hold; no anatomical detail or animated wounds.
rules.measurable_as: Judgement; the state change completes in under 1 s on its keyword.

rules.rule: Lock the camera by default; meaning comes from change inside the frame, in the drawing (morph, transform, draw-on, redraw), not from moving the whole picture.
rules.measurable_as: Share of shots with no camera move 0.76 to 0.86 per batch (607 of 799 to 815 of 945); flag a lesson below about 0.7. The lowest per-film share in batch 08 was 0.58, and two batch 02 films never move. transform_into, morph and draw_on appear in 11 to 12 of 12 films (batch 05).

rules.rule: When the camera moves, it makes one slow move on one axis (push, pull, pan, tilt or truck) that eases and settles; no handheld, shake, whip or compound moves, and a shake is kept for a single shock.
rules.measurable_as: Per shot: at most one move segment, one dominant axis, no direction reversal or velocity spike; compound 'multiple' camera tags in only 2 to 6 shots per batch; shake in at most one shot per film.

rules.rule: Use a push-in to isolate or emphasise a named subject and a pull-out to reveal scale or context; pans, tilts and follows are rarer and kept for reading a row or a reveal.
rules.measurable_as: Push-in and pull-out are the leading moves in most batches (push_in 31 to 57 and pull_out 12 to 62 shots per batch; which one leads varies, and batch 06 also has 46 right pans); each move is tagged reveal or focus in the storyboard.

rules.rule: Tie each move to the narration: a push starts on the noun that names its target and holds once framed; a reveal move ends on the word it reveals.
rules.measurable_as: Timeline against Loom word timings: push start or reveal end inside the keyword's interval, followed by a static hold. In the films this timing is the vision model's description, not a measured offset.

rules.rule: The hard cut is the default join, on the narration beat.
rules.measurable_as: Hard cuts are 0.63 to 0.79 of joins per batch and 0.53 to 0.93 per film in batch 08. These counts include boundaries between sub-shots of one long shot, which are not real joins, so treat them as approximate.

rules.rule: Every gradual join carries a meaning tied to the content: morph for becoming or idea to idea, zoom-through for entering a place, layer or scale, dissolve or redraw for passing time or emotion, a shaped wipe or iris for a chapter, topic reset or caused change, a pan for travelling along a list or between scales. Gradual joins sit at section, world or scale boundaries; inside a scene the beats are hard cuts.
rules.measurable_as: Each non-cut join carries a meaning tag in the storyboard and coincides with a section, world, time or scale change; joins at segment boundaries are gradual more often than joins inside segments.

rules.rule: Build a gradual join out of what is in the frame: the outgoing subject becomes the next (morph, object transform), a departing object, an opening or a portal carries the eye, or the wipe is cut from the subject's own material. Thematic wipes are fast.
rules.measurable_as: Judgement at each non-cut join: name the element that persists or drives the change, and fail when none is named; the same shape and colour in the last frame of shot n and the first frame of shot n+1; wipe_in median 0.63 s (batch 03).

rules.rule: Plain dissolves and fades through black are rare: a dissolve marks time, links a person to a place or releases emotion, and a fade through black is one quiet breath before a final or darker turn, about once per film at most. Some of the films' dissolves hold a deliberate ghost of the outgoing shot; Loom's double-exposure check at joins would flag that, so it is a gate conflict to resolve, not a defect of the films.
rules.measurable_as: Dissolves 4 to 26 joins per batch of 529 to 1068 (under 3 percent); fade_through_black 1 to 4 per batch; flag more than 2 fades per lesson (batch 03).

rules.rule: When the subject stays the same, change the picture in place (redraw, swap, add, or hold and change on the same ground) instead of cutting to a new scene.
rules.measurable_as: Judgement on consecutive beats about the same subject. The records' none_continuous join counts cannot support this rule numerically, because many of them fall on boundaries between sub-shots of one long shot.

rules.rule: Pick a tempo family and hold it through the film: slow diagram films cut about 5 to 6 times a minute, fast story films 12 to 15 or more, and most films sit near 8 to 13.
rules.measurable_as: Code cuts per minute per film: batch medians 8.3 to 15.0; per-film p10 to p90 about 4 to 20 across batches. Outliers: 3.89 (BSdEiOYvKpE, detector likely missed redraws) and 30.67 (HDt_rTPPh70); jLOuMXnM5wk has 0 detected cuts and its pacing is unknown.

rules.rule: Speed up through lists, examples and action montages (shots of about 1 to 3 s) and slow down at definitions, mechanisms, data and key images (about 5 to 18 s). Sub-second bursts stay short and are followed by a longer shot.
rules.measurable_as: Mean shot length of define, explain_mechanism and diagram beats exceeds the film median, and example, list and story_beat beats fall below it; runs of shots under 1 to 1.5 s last at most about 3 shots or 10 s outside a montage.

rules.rule: Keep something meaningful moving in most seconds, even with a locked camera.
rules.measurable_as: Code motion share per film: batch medians 0.72 to 0.95, p10 0.60 to 0.82; flag a lesson below about 0.6. The share comes from frame change, so grain and compression may lift it; check against the frames.

rules.rule: Still holds are short and purposeful: spend them on the key line, a definition, a finished diagram, a symbol or the end card, not on story beats. Most films keep their longest motionless stretch near 5 s, but some hold 10 to 24 s. Loom's static-hold check would flag those long holds; that is a gate conflict to resolve, not a defect of the films.
rules.measurable_as: Code over all holds: longest still stretch per film median 5 s, maximum 24 s, over 10 s in 10 of 96 films (the batch figures of a 4 to 8 s median came from hold lists truncated at six entries). Tag each hold over about 8 s as define, symbol, diagram, release or credits.

rules.rule: Build a diagram on one held page: the background and placed elements stay still while new parts arrive, so a mechanism build can run 10 to 18 s on one frame provided something is added every few seconds. Diagram beats are the longest in a film and character beats cut short.
rules.measurable_as: Within a diagram shot, existing elements do not move while new ones are added; shots over 10 s contain a new element or state change at least every 4 s (batch 04); full-frame diagram examples run 15.6 to 18.2 s (batch 07).

rules.rule: Narrate at a calm explainer rate, about 125 to 160 words per minute.
rules.measurable_as: Words per minute per film: batch medians 129 to 161; per-film p10 to p90 about 116 to 182.

rules.rule: Open on a silent card (the brand mark alone in its colour on a plain field, often with a single quote) and start the narration only after it, at about 6 to 8.7 s; the picture speaks first.
rules.measurable_as: First word time about 6.0 to 8.7 s in nearly every film (10 to 12 of 12 per batch); no speech in the first 6 s. Exceptions are live-host or hybrid films (UDdkgOoeNcQ at 0.85 s; one batch 02 film at 1.17 s).

rules.rule: Entrances are short and eased: pops and fades about half a second, slides about 0.6 to 0.9 s, scale-ins about 0.7 to 0.9 s, draw-ons up to about a second.
rules.measurable_as: Batch medians: pop_in 0.40 to 0.58 s, fade_in 0.5 to 0.7 s, slide_in 0.63 to 0.88 s, scale_in 0.67 to 0.92 s, draw_on 0.67 to 1.08 s; flag an entrance outside its type's batch p10 to p90 band (pop_in 0.13 to 1.84 s in batch 01).

rules.rule: Exits are short and finish before the next idea arrives; usually they are no longer than the matching entrance, so the stage clears first.
rules.measurable_as: Exit medians: exit_fade 0.38 to 0.7 s, exit_scale 0.42 to 0.92 s, exit_slide 0.6 to 0.92 s; outgoing elements are gone before the incoming element finishes. Batches disagree on slides and scales (exit slide slower than slide-in in batches 01, 05 and 06), so exit-faster is usual, not universal.

rules.rule: Transformations take about a second, longer than entrances, with a hold before and after; morphs between unlike shapes take longer.
rules.measurable_as: morph median 0.71 to 1.5 s across batches (p75 up to 2.5 s); transform_into median 0.71 to 1.29 s; still frames before and after the change.

rules.rule: Ease every authored move: arrivals ease out, falls, tips and plunges ease in, and ease-in-out is the most common shape; the speed peak sits near the middle of the move or a little before.
rules.measurable_as: Code move shapes per batch: ease_in_out about 640 to 1080, ease_out about 460 to 660, ease_in about 320 to 390; ease_out median 0.67 to 0.96 s and ease_in 0.83 to 1.38 s; move peak at a median 0.43 to 0.5 of the move. Ignore the code's 'linear' moves (median 0.13 s): they are measurement jitter, not authored motion.

rules.rule: Most motion carries the idea; staging, transition, ambient and emphasis motion support it, and ambient motion never outweighs content in a scene.
rules.measurable_as: Motion meaning tags: content is the largest class in every batch (953 to 1318 events; about 0.4 of all tagged motion in batch 08); flag scenes where ambient motion exceeds content motion.

rules.rule: Keep a held shot alive with one slow ambient layer while the subject stays still; ambient loops are long, low in contrast, off the focal object and never the fastest thing in frame.
rules.measurable_as: Ambient loop period median 3.0 to 5.2 s across batches (p25 1.6 to 2.75 s); static shots over about 2 to 3 s contain one looping element; moving pixels in held shots sit in one layer below the subject's contrast.

rules.rule: Build a set by staggered arrivals, one member per spoken item, never a finished set or diagram presented at once.
rules.measurable_as: In a group reveal, entrance onsets differ and each aligns to its word; no more than about 2 new elements in any 0.5 s window unless they are a staggered set (batch 04); pop_in is the most common entrance (262 events in all 12 films of batch 06).

rules.rule: Each new element, label, number or change lands on the word that names it.
rules.measurable_as: Loom-side check with TTS word timings: entry or landing frame inside the naming word's interval (batch rules give windows of 0 to 0.5 s). In the films this is observed, not measured: the vision model labelled picture and speech as coinciding in about nine of ten shots (572 of 640 to 1002 of 1068 per batch), and the offsets it wrote are not measurements. Whether entrances lead the word slightly (records describe 0.2 to 0.5 s early) or never precede it (batch 04) is unsettled.

rules.rule: Within a beat, show the thing first and let its label or number land on it; in a mechanism, the cause completes before its labels or result appear.
rules.measurable_as: Label onset follows the object onset in the same shot; in mechanism beats, label start is at or after the end of the cause motion.

rules.rule: The decisive change completes on the result word, and a counter settles on the spoken figure, not at the start of the sentence.
rules.measurable_as: End of the morph or transform within a beat of the result word; counter final value equals the spoken number and lands within 0.5 s of it.

rules.rule: Cut and move on the narration, not on a music or effects grid: only about a third of cuts and moves land on a sound hit.
rules.measurable_as: Code: cuts-on-hit share batch medians 0.29 to 0.37 (p10 to p90 about 0.23 to 0.5); moves-on-hit 0.35 to 0.40.

rules.rule: Keep the music bed a few dB under the voice.
rules.measurable_as: Code bed_below_speech: batch medians 5.6 to 6.8 dB, p10 to p90 about 2.8 to 9.2 dB. What the code measure means exactly is unsettled, so compare like with like.

rules.rule: No narration over the brand open or the credits, and let a few wordless stretches (cold open, release beats, credits) breathe on music alone. Loom's empty-frame check would flag the near-empty rest beats some films use here; that is a gate conflict to resolve, not a defect of the films.
rules.measurable_as: no_speech shots sit on brand cards, transitions, release beats and credits (20 shots across 9 films in batch 05; 56 of 1003 shots in batch 08).

rules.rule: Keep shots simple: about five elements per shot, rarely more than about twelve, in two or at most three flat depth planes.
rules.measurable_as: Elements per shot: batch medians 4 to 6, p90 8 to 12; depth layers median 2 and p90 3 in every batch. Flag frames above about 12 elements outside a repeated-icon field, crowd, grid or contained panel.

rules.rule: One idea per shot: one subject, one change and one label at a time; clear the frame before the next idea so two explanation groups never animate together.
rules.measurable_as: Simultaneous independent changes per shot at most 1 outside lists; no two explanation groups animate in the same time window; one function tag per shot.

rules.rule: Show numbers and data as picture: repeated units, grids, counters, rise-and-fall cycles, a comparison with a familiar object, or a big numeral on an object, rather than axis charts; a chart, if any, is a short summary after the enacted version.
rules.measurable_as: Data-visualisation shots only 2 to 5 per batch; share of data beats using a picture device versus a chart template.

rules.rule: Turn a spoken list into pictures that build one item per spoken item, in place, and clear together before an exception or the next idea; never bullets.
rules.measurable_as: n staggered entrances bound to n words; frame cleared before the next list; list-type text at most about 1 percent of text items (3 of 506 in batch 08).

rules.rule: Centre the subject by default; use thirds and diagonals for action, travel and character beats, and symmetry for authority, formality and pairs.
rules.measurable_as: Composition tags: centred is the largest class in seven of eight batches (0.41 to 0.49 of shots); batch 06 has thirds slightly ahead (390 against 351 centred); focal centroid in the central third in about 40 to 50 percent of shots.

rules.rule: Give the subject real negative space: medium by default, high for definitions, establishing shots and lone objects; low negative space and crowded frames are exceptions.
rules.measurable_as: Negative space medium or high in about 0.7 to 0.9 of shots per batch (490 of 640, 717 of 1003, 472 of 529); crowded composition in 13 of 702 shots (batch 04) and 25 of 529 (batch 05).

rules.rule: Lay out comparisons and opposed pairs as equal, mirrored panels or a symmetric split with a thin seam, identical in scale and pose so one variable differs; labels land after the split.
rules.measurable_as: Panel widths equal within 2 percent and figure heights within 5 percent (batch 01); subject centroids mirror about the vertical centre within 0.05 of width (batch 03); symmetric compositions in 66 shots across 11 films and split screens in 17 shots across 8 films (batch 02).

rules.rule: Use a frame within the frame (door, window, screen, lens, card, arch, spotlight, torn border) to isolate a subject, contain dense material, mark something as entered, observed or reported, or direct the eye in place of arrows.
rules.measurable_as: frame_within_frame in 26 to 58 shots per batch, across 7 to 11 films; the focal cue comes from framing or isolation rather than arrows (judgement).

rules.rule: Build a few linked worlds with fixed jobs (the story world, an evidence desk, an interior or abstract world) rather than one continuous set or a new look per scene; re-enter each by the same move and keep finish, palette and drawing language constant across them.
rules.measurable_as: About 3 or fewer worlds per lesson; each crossing is a gradual join or carries a shared motif or the accent. The records label nearly every film few_worlds_linked, which batch 05 suspects is a default label, so judge it on the storyboard.

rules.rule: Thread the film with a recurring object or motif that crosses settings and sections (a passport, a dashed route, a window, a map, an accent object), and return to a human anchor between technical sections.
rules.measurable_as: At least one motif recurs in 3 or more segments; the records list about 6 to 8 recurring motifs per film (batches 05 and 06).

rules.rule: The finish (grain, paper, crayon, brush, stipple, or clean flat fills) and the shading model are a family choice made once: apply them to every layer for the whole film so mixed media reads as one world, and never switch mid-film. Texture is not a house constant: one batch found paper or grain in all 12 films while two others found no texture on most shots.
rules.measurable_as: Texture and shading class per shot constant within a lesson; texture none on 949 of 1068 shots (batch 06) and 621 of 945 (batch 07) against texture in all 12 films of batch 02. Judge grain on the encoded video, since 854x480 compression may mimic it.

rules.rule: Backgrounds stay plain: a solid field or dark void isolates symbols, definitions and diagrams, and illustrated scenes are kept for story; no detailed environment or gradient sky behind a diagram.
rules.measurable_as: Solid plus dark-void backgrounds on about 0.4 to 0.5 of shots (257 of 640 in batch 01, 330 of 621 in batch 03, 358 of 702 in batch 04); illustrated scenes about a quarter to a third (286 of 945 in batch 07); symbol and define beats use a solid or void field.

avoid.anti_pattern: Moving the camera for energy or for its own sake: handheld shake, whip pans, orbits, drift, compound moves in one shot, pans as connective motion, or tracking a subject to show speed.
avoid.why: The camera is locked in about three quarters or more of shots and moves once, slowly, to reveal, focus or change scale; a moving lens on moving content loses the reading frame. Speed is shown by moving the background behind a fixed subject.

avoid.anti_pattern: Two or more unrelated saturated accents competing in one frame.
avoid.why: The single accent on the named element is the main focal cue in every batch; a second accent splits the eye and makes the frame read like a slide or a poster. Several hues appear only as a coded set, the two sides of a comparison, a title or end tableau, or a deliberate abundance or chaos beat.

avoid.anti_pattern: Lip-synced dialogue and detailed or realistic facial acting on drawn characters.
avoid.why: An off-screen narrator does the talking and posture carries emotion; lip sync appears in only a handful of shots per batch, nearly all live action, and detailed faces compete with the accent and break the minimal design.

avoid.anti_pattern: Bullet lists, sentences, paragraphs or caption strips that restate the narration.
avoid.why: Text is a label, term or number and the picture does the explaining; lists become pictures that build one item per spoken item, and text that must be read in full lives on an artefact in the world. List text appears in only a few shots per batch.

avoid.anti_pattern: Axis charts, floating number captions or bare abstract diagrams as the main carrier of a number or a mechanism.
avoid.why: Numbers ride objects (tags, counters, units, queues) and get a picture anchor when spoken; data-visualisation shots are 2 to 5 per batch, and even data beats carry an enacting figure, object or place.

avoid.anti_pattern: Text that cannot be read: loose over a busy or textured scene, over a face, under about 0.03 of frame height, or in a decorative script the audience cannot read.
avoid.why: Labels sit on objects, tags or backings beside the subject; text under 0.03 of frame height is UI texture, signage or credits only, and a write-on device still needs legible type.

avoid.anti_pattern: Crossfades, plain dissolves or fades through black as the routine join between scenes.
avoid.why: Hard cuts carry the rhythm and gradual joins carry a meaning; dissolves are under 3 percent of joins and fades through black one to four per batch. The few deliberate ghost-hold dissolves would trip Loom's double-exposure check at joins, which is a gate conflict to resolve, not a licence to use more of them.

avoid.anti_pattern: Generic or one-off effect transitions (spins, flips, star wipes) with no idea in them, or outside the film's own small set of joins.
avoid.why: Joins are made from material in the frame and each film keeps a small join grammar; a stray effect reads as a template trick.

avoid.anti_pattern: A frozen frame with nothing moving and nothing new to read while the voice runs on.
avoid.why: Motion share is high in every batch, and holds are spent on a key line, a definition, a diagram or the end card, usually with an ambient layer. The code over all holds puts the longest still per film at a median of 5 s, but 10 of 96 films hold over 10 s (up to 24 s), so length alone does not make a hold a defect; Loom's static-hold check has to allow a deliberate one.

avoid.anti_pattern: Pictures, labels or changes that ignore the sentence being spoken, arrive after their word has passed, or linger after the idea.
avoid.why: Word-bound change is the spine of these films; the vision model labels only a few percent of shots unrelated (mostly breathers, transitions and end cards) and almost none lagging. This is the model's description, not a measured offset.

avoid.anti_pattern: Mixing registers or finishes without a shared treatment: raw photos or footage, 3D, gloss or gradient-shaded figures as the base layer, a texture or ground change between cuts, or a hard cut into a new register with nothing carried across.
avoid.why: One finish and flat shading hold the world together; photo, footage and 3D appear as brief inserts that are framed, tinted or graded and bracketed by a marked join, otherwise they read as pasted in.

avoid.anti_pattern: Visual vocabulary that does not belong: stock clip-art icons, a concept redrawn with a new icon or colour between shots, or a new character for a state change of the same person.
avoid.why: Every icon is drawn in the film's own hand; one token design and fixed colour meanings let the viewer track an idea across worlds, and the same figure morphs or swaps pose so identity carries.

avoid.anti_pattern: Individually animated crowds, long full-body animation, or walk cycles as the main source of motion.
avoid.why: Crowds are repeated glyphs and acting is short gestures (character_act median about 0.5 to 1 s); walk cycles are about 17 to 20 events per batch, mostly for journeys and chases, because walking costs time and shows nothing.

avoid.anti_pattern: Graphic or anatomical depiction of death, injury or violence.
avoid.why: Harm is symbolic: one snappy motion, a flat red mark, a burst, X eyes, a flash or a fade; this stays readable and suits wide and employee audiences.

avoid.anti_pattern: Juvenile, gross-out or horror set pieces as the payoff of a beat, and real trademarks, song lyrics or attributed quotes reproduced on screen.
avoid.why: The records' own notes flag these gags as wrong for adults at work even where the films use them: keep the device and drop the gag. Trademarks, lyrics and quotes are content, not technique, and cannot be reused in client work.

avoid.anti_pattern: Building in the wrong order: a finished diagram with every label at once, two ideas animating together, labels piling up into a legend or a key with leader lines, or a scene that starts from an empty frame and assembles everything on screen.
avoid.why: Parts arrive on their words in staggered waves onto a composed scene, labels sit on what they name and clear after their clause, and one idea animates at a time. Loom's empty-frame check agrees about empty starts, but it would also flag the deliberate near-empty rest beats some films use.

avoid.anti_pattern: Crowded frames with little negative space, and detailed, outlined or high-contrast backgrounds competing with figures or sitting behind diagrams.
avoid.why: Negative space is medium or high in most shots; when density is needed it is contained in a frame or grid, or used on purpose to show a crowd problem, and backgrounds stay flat, low in contrast or single-hue so the subject reads first.

avoid.anti_pattern: Starting the narration on frame one or over the opening card.
avoid.why: Nearly every film keeps a silent opening card and starts speaking at about 6 to 8.7 s; the exceptions are live-host or hybrid films.

avoid.anti_pattern: Lower-third name bars, and identity labels that stay on screen through the content.
avoid.why: People are named by a badge, nameplate or hand-drawn banner in the art on the spoken name, and it leaves before the speaker's point.

avoid.anti_pattern: Emphasis devices used continuously: constant particles and sparkle, or sub-second cutting sustained through a whole film.
avoid.why: Particles and fast bursts are punctuation at peaks; most films keep a per-film median shot of 2.8 to 4.6 s (batch 08), and one film at 1.4 s shots and 30.67 cuts per minute is the outlier.

judge_rubric.name: Composition and focus
judge_rubric.question: Name the style first. Does each frame give the eye one clear subject, placed on purpose, with the rest of the frame subordinate, as the best frames of that style do?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Several elements of equal size, brightness and colour scattered edge to edge; no subject; or a slide layout (title on top, a block of text or icons below); text overlaps the subject.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: A subject can be found, but a second bright element or busy background competes; everything centred by habit with even margins; empty areas look left over rather than designed.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: One subject, centred, on a third or on a strong diagonal, carrying the only saturated accent; about four to six elements; a framing device (light pool, lens, window, monitor, panel seam) leads the eye; dense material sits inside a container or grid; a deliberately empty rest frame or a wide field around a tiny subject counts as composed, not empty.

judge_rubric.name: Legibility
judge_rubric.question: Can every word, number and shape meant to be read be read at a glance at delivery size, against its own field?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Labels under about 0.03 of frame height, thin type on busy texture, sentences or bullet lists on screen, text over faces, or labels that flash off before they can be read.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: Readable, but sizes are uniform (numbers no bigger than labels), contrast is weak on some fields, fonts are mixed or generic, or text lingers after its clause.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: One to three words per text block; labels about 0.05 of frame height sitting on or pointing to what they name; titles about 0.12 or larger; key numbers about 0.12 to 0.18, larger than labels and alone; high contrast on a quiet area; lettering consistent with the style (hand, serif, monospace or clean sans all qualify); text clears when its job is done.

judge_rubric.name: Visual explanation
judge_rubric.question: Does the picture itself carry the idea (mechanism, quantity, comparison, scale), so the point survives with the sound off?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Generic icons or stock-like scenes beside the words, or text cards restating the narration; the frame would fit any script; numbers only as captions.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: Literal illustration of the nouns spoken; a relevant diagram exists but sits still while the voice explains the cause, change or difference.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: A visible device for each claim: a cutaway or cross-section where one part changes on its word, a count as repeated objects with an accented subset, a number written on a familiar object, a pull-back from one unit to the crowd, matched before and after on identical geometry, a lens or zoom-through to the hidden scale, a wrong model struck or morphed into the right one in place.

judge_rubric.name: Motion with purpose
judge_rubric.question: Is each movement a change that means something (arrival, transformation, cause, emphasis), timed and eased, with the rest of the frame calm?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Everything bounces, floats or spins at once; robotic linear slides; the camera drifts for no reason; motion unrelated to the words.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: Tidy but uniform: every element enters the same way; the meaningful change is not clearly the main event; some decorative motion competes with the subject.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: One main event per beat (a draw-on, a morph, a stamp, a gesture, an impact then hold); short eased entrances (pop about 0.4 to 0.6 s, slide under 1 s), transformations about 0.7 to 1.2 s then a hold; exits quicker than entrances; one slow ambient loop keeps a hold alive; a still subject while the world moves is a valid choice; a deliberate rest beat with almost nothing moving is pacing, not a defect.

judge_rubric.name: Continuity of joins
judge_rubric.question: Do shots link into one argument, with the join chosen to match the kind of change?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Arbitrary effect wipes or spins between unrelated frames; palette, scale or drawing style jumps with no reason; a subject jumps position between related beats; visible seams or elements popping out mid-move.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: Clean hard cuts and a consistent look, but nothing carries across; every gradual join is the same generic transition whatever the change.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: Hard cuts on phrase boundaries inside an idea; at a change of idea the outgoing subject becomes the next (a morph, a carried object, a push through an opening, a wipe made of the scene's own material); a deliberate dissolve or brief ghost hold marks time, memory or a gentle cut and is judged as intended; one ground, motif or token returns across distant scenes; the ending can call back to the opening.

judge_rubric.name: Style consistency
judge_rubric.question: Name the style first (sketch line, storybook outline, cut paper, dark void, glow technical, geometric flat, corporate flat, live hybrid). Is that one style executed fully in every frame?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Mixed icon families, line weights or shading models with no reason; clean stock vector pasted into a drawn world; inserts that look pasted in; colours that change meaning; looks like a template whatever the genre.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: One recognisable style with lapses: an off-model prop, a scene that drops the outline or texture rule, a second accent creeping in, or details that look taken from a kit.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: One outline rule, one fill and shading model, one finish and one lettering hand across every shot, diagrams and cards included; one accent with one meaning; a deliberate register break (a dark void, a neon interlude, a live insert, a studio outro) is short, bracketed by a clear join and consistent within itself, and counts as design, not a style mix.

judge_rubric.name: Pacing
judge_rubric.question: Does the rhythm follow meaning: quick through lists and turns, held where something must be read or felt?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Every shot the same length; or stretches over about 8 s where nothing changes and nothing is meant to be read; or relentless sub-second cutting that leaves labels unread.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: A reasonable average (shots around 3 to 5 s) but flat: definitions, lists and emotional beats get the same time.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: A chosen tempo held within the film (slow paper-diagram films and fast story films both qualify); 1 to 3 s beats through lists and montage peaks; 5 to 15 s builds where something is added every few seconds; a held key line or a wordless release beat after a dense idea; a calm open and an ending that slows into the close.

judge_rubric.name: Polish and finish
judge_rubric.question: Is the frame finished to a professional level a corporate client could hand to its employees, within its own style?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Looks like a slide or an amateur template: default fonts and shapes, aliased or uneven strokes, misaligned elements, placeholder text, half-built frames, jitter.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: Clean and tidy but plain: sterile vector where the style wants surface, or a texture that looks like a filter laid on top; generic easing; a thrown-together end card.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: Every frame worth pausing on: crafted custom shapes, a deliberate finish that suits the style and survives compression (paper, grain, halftone, glow, or a clean flat surface for a clean style), soft vignettes or light where used, small lived-in details, composed from the first frame of each shot, a tidy designed close.

judge_rubric.name: Character
judge_rubric.question: When people or personified agents appear, are they designed for the style and acted with economy, in a tone that suits adult employees?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Stiff stock or bean figures, inconsistent designs between shots, detailed but lifeless faces, constant fidgeting, or babyish mascots and gross-out gags in an adult lesson.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: Consistent simple figures who mostly stand beside the idea; poses do not change with the narration; crowds drawn as many individuals acting at once.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: Few figures per shot, one design grammar for the cast; emotion carried by posture, one feature or one gesture that peaks on the keyword; a persistent agent tracked in one colour; crowds as repeated figures or silhouettes around one active subject; a hand that enters to act and leaves; neutral, professional tone. Frames with no character score on the other questions, not here.

judge_rubric.name: Sync with narration
judge_rubric.question: Do visible changes land on the words that name them, and clear before the next idea?
judge_rubric.anchor_1: Elements appear seconds before they are named or long after; whole lists appear at once; counters stop on a different number than the one spoken; overlays linger into the next idea.
judge_rubric.anchor_3: Shots change on sentence boundaries, but events inside the shot are loosely timed or arrive a clause early.
judge_rubric.anchor_5: Each pop, label, morph, gesture and stamp completes on its naming or result word; lists build one item per spoken item; counters settle on the spoken figure; cuts sit on phrase boundaries; overlays clear before the next idea.

open_questions: Sync lead: sync_offset_s is a value the vision model wrote (0.0 for 6,116 of 6,307 shots), not a measurement, and frames were sampled near 1 fps. Do entrances really lead the word by 0.2 to 0.5 s, as many records describe? Measure against word timings on full-frame-rate video before any sync gate uses a number.

Morph or dissolve: how many of the morphs and object-transform joins (the batch records report morphs in at least 48 of the 60 films of batches 01, 03, 05, 07 and 08) are true outline interpolations rather than dissolves or fast cuts sampled at 1 fps? This decides the priority of a path-morph primitive.

Grain and paper strength: how much of the texture is artwork and how much is 480p compression? Check a few films at full resolution before moving Loom's finish default (grain near off, D-100) toward visible strength.

One accent or one dominant accent: every record claims one saturated accent per frame, yet several shots describe two. A per-frame chroma cluster count with hex values is needed before an accent gate can be calibrated.
Line boil: is the hand-line flicker in the sketch and wobbly families real frame-to-frame boil or compression shimmer? If it is static wobble, the existing seeded rough.js sketch mode may be enough.

Pacing on redraw films: the cut detector misses redraw-in-place changes (jLOuMXnM5wk has 0 detected cuts; several films are split into equal sub-shot windows), and shot-list boundaries and detected joins disagree both ways. Which source should pacing rules use, and what are the true longest holds per film?

Live and talk formats: should the 10 live or stage films (live_action_hybrid) count toward house constants and pacing targets, or be a separate format? They break the silent open, the single narrator and the pacing ranges.

Gate conflicts: Loom's double-exposure warning (loom/qa.py) exempts only 'continue' joins on one station, so it would flag deliberate ghost-hold dissolves; the empty-frame check (loom/checks/film.py) errors unless the beat intent is hold, sparse or dark. Should a dissolve or ghost hold get its own declared intent, and should rest beats be declared by default in packs that use them?

Judge calibration: the same vision model condemned 35 % of clean windows of real films (mostly crossfades, style mixes, motion jank and static holds). Does this style-aware rubric, with deliberate dissolves and rest beats written into the 5 anchors, cut those false condemnations without losing recall on planted defects? Re-run the 493 clean windows and the planted set.

Sound: no sound records were made. What does the 4.3 to 7.9 dB 'bed below speech' figure measure, and which visual events carry the sparse non-speech hits (about 5 per minute)? No sound rule should be built until a sound pass runs.
